verses.text: Samuel died; and all Israel gathered themselves together, and mourned for him, and buried him at his house at Ramah. Then David arose, and went down to the wilderness of Paran.
There was a man in Maon, whose possessions were in Carmel; and the man was very great. He had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats; and he was shearing his sheep in Carmel.
Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail. This woman was intelligent and had a beautiful face; but the man was surly and evil in his doings. He was of the house of Caleb.
David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his sheep.
David sent ten young men, and David said to the young men, “Go up to Carmel, and go to Nabal, and greet him in my name.
Tell him, ‘Long life to you! Peace be to you, and peace be to your house, and peace be to all that you have.
Now I have heard that you have shearers. Your shepherds have now been with us, and we didn’t harm them, neither was there anything missing from them, all the while they were in Carmel.

Ask your young men, and they will tell you. Therefore let the young men find favor in your eyes; for we come on a good day. Please give whatever comes to your hand, to your servants, and to your son David.’”
When David’s young men came, they spoke to Nabal all those words in the name of David, and waited.
Nabal answered David’s servants, and said, “Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants who break away from their masters these days.
Shall I then take my bread, my water, and my meat that I have killed for my shearers, and give it to men who I don’t know where they come from?”
So David’s young men turned on their way, and went back, and came and told him all these words.
David said to his men, “Every man put on his sword!” Every man put on his sword. David also put on his sword. About four hundred men followed David, and two hundred stayed by the baggage.
But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal’s wife, saying, “Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to Greet our master; and he insulted them.
But the men were very good to us, and we were not harmed, and we didn’t miss anything, as long as we went with them, when we were in the fields.
They were a wall to us both by night and by day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep.
Now therefore know and consider what you will do; for evil is determined against our master, and against all his house; for he is such a worthless fellow that one can’t speak to him.”

Then Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves of bread, two bottles of wine, five sheep ready dressed, five seahs  of parched grain, one hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on donkeys.
She said to her young men, “Go on before me. Behold, I am coming after you.” But she didn’t tell her husband, Nabal.
As she rode on her donkey, and came down by the covert of the mountain, that behold, David and his men came down toward her, and she met them.
Now David had said, “Surely in vain I have kept all that this fellow has in the wilderness, so that nothing was missed of all that pertained to him. He has returned me evil for good.
God do so to the enemies of David, and more also, if I leave of all that belongs to him by the morning light so much as one who urinates on a wall.”
When Abigail saw David, she hurried and got off of her donkey, and fell before David on her face, and bowed herself to the ground.
She fell at his feet, and said, “On me, my lord, on me be the blame! Please let your servant speak in your ears. Hear the words of your servant.

Please don’t let my lord pay attention to this worthless fellow, Nabal; for as his name is, so is he. Nabal  is his name, and folly is with him; but I, your servant, didn’t see my lord’s young men, whom you sent.

Now therefore, my lord, as Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, since Yahweh has withheld you from blood guiltiness, and from avenging yourself with your own hand, now therefore let your enemies, and those who seek evil to my lord, be as Nabal.
Now this present which your servant has brought to my lord, let it be given to the young men who follow my lord.
Please forgive the trespass of your servant. For Yahweh will certainly make my lord a sure house, because my lord fights Yahweh’s battles. Evil will not be found in you all your days.

Though men may rise up to pursue you, and to seek your soul, yet the soul of my lord will be bound in the bundle of life with Yahweh your God. He will sling out the souls of your enemies, as from the hollow of a sling.
It will come to pass, when Yahweh has done to my lord according to all the good that he has spoken concerning you, and has appointed you prince over Israel,

that this shall be no grief to you, nor offense of heart to my lord, either that you have shed blood without cause, or that my lord has avenged himself. When Yahweh has dealt well with my lord, then remember your servant.”
David said to Abigail, “Blessed is Yahweh, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me!
Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand.

For indeed, as Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, who has withheld me from harming you, unless you had hurried and come to meet me, surely there wouldn’t have been left to Nabal by the morning light so much as one who urinates on a wall.”
So David received from her hand that which she had brought him. Then he said to her, “Go up in peace to your house. Behold, I have listened to your voice, and have granted your request.”

Abigail came to Nabal; and behold, he held a feast in his house, like the feast of a king. Nabal’s heart was merry within him, for he was very drunk. Therefore she told him nothing, until the morning light.
In the morning, when the wine had gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone.
About ten days later, Yahweh struck Nabal, so that he died.

When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, “Blessed is Yahweh, who has pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal, and has kept back his servant from evil. Yahweh has returned the evildoing of Nabal on his own head.” David sent and spoke concerning Abigail, to take her to himself as wife.
When David’s servants had come to Abigail to Carmel, they spoke to her, saying, “David has sent us to you, to take you to him as wife.”
She arose, and bowed herself with her face to the earth, and said, “Behold, your servant is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.”
Abigail hurried, and arose, and rode on a donkey, with five ladies of hers who followed her; and she went after the messengers of David, and became his wife.
David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel; and they both became his wives.
Now Saul had given Michal his daughter, David’s wife, to Palti the son of Laish, who was of Gallim.

footnotes.content: Samuel, the great shepherd of Israel, has gone home to be with the Lord. When someone like that is gone, the wound feels like the sky has dimmed. David moves into the wilderness, away from Saul's shadow and into his own deep time with God—learning things only solitude and exile can teach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nabal—a man of Carmel, enormously rich: three thousand sheep, a thousand goats. He is shearing his flocks, the busiest, most prosperous hour of the year. His wealth is visible, impressive, real. But wealth says nothing about what lives inside a man.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: See the marriage of contrasts: Abigail—intelligent, beautiful, gracious; Nabal—surly, crude, worthless. Sometimes God places a wise heart in the same house as a foolish one, so that wisdom may have a chance to save the day when folly runs out of rope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: News travels fast in the desert. David hears that Nabal is shearing his flocks—and David's men, protecting those very flocks all summer, have gone hungry in the wilderness. It seems a small thing to ask for provisions in return for faithful service.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David is still learning what it means to lead. He sends ten young men with a courteous greeting—the way a man in his position might. He is not king yet; he is testing the boundaries of influence and grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Long life to you. Peace be to you." David's greeting is warm and proper. He is asking not for favor, but offering it first—the hallmark of someone who has learned something true about power and courtesy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David lays out the truth simply: his men have protected Nabal's shepherds all summer. Nothing stolen, no one harmed. It is the language of a man who has done honest work and expects honest recognition in return.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You come on a good day." It is the season of rejoicing, the harvest home of wool. David is asking, in effect: on your best day, when your heart is full, will you remember the men who kept this prosperity safe?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ten men speak in David's name and wait. There is a moment of silence here—a space where courtesy and grace might have taken root, if there had been soil for them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nabal's answer is contempt wrapped in a question. 'Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse?' He does not recognize kindness or debt. His refusal is not just unkind—it is a kind of blindness to the good others have done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nabal clings to his bread, his water, his meat as though they belong to him alone. But a generous man knows that provision is a trust, not a fortress. Nabal's refusal will cost him far more than a meal would have.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The young men return with their report. David hears rejection and scorn where he offered courtesy. The wound is deep because it came dressed as contempt, not simple need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's first instinct is anger, the natural consequence of pride struck. He arms his men—four hundred warriors ready to move. In this moment, David is not yet the man God means him to be. He is about to teach a violent lesson.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One of the young men tells Abigail what happened. He speaks the truth plainly: David's kindness was met with insult. The servant sees what Nabal cannot: that an angry man is on his way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The servants attest: 'The men were very good to us. We were not harmed.' This is what Nabal refused to hear. The truth of faithful service, spoken by those who received it, stands as a quiet rebuke to his pride.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "They were a wall to us both by night and by day." This ancient image speaks volumes—like a fortress, like faithful guardians. The protection was constant, visible, real. And Nabal saw it all, and chose to forget it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The servants urgently tell Abigail: 'Evil is determined against our master.' They see the danger coming. They know Nabal will not listen to reason—he is a 'worthless fellow.' But they trust that Abigail can understand what he cannot.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abigail acts at once. She gathers provisions—bread, wine, meat, grain, fruit. Not a grudging gift, but a generous one. She understands what Nabal does not: that sometimes the cost of a gift is far less than the cost of pride.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abigail sends the gifts on ahead and tells the servants she is coming after. But she does not tell Nabal. She acts with quiet urgency, the way a woman acts when she sees death coming and knows her husband is too drunk on his own importance to help himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abigail rides down from the mountains on her donkey and meets David and his men coming toward her. It is a moment arranged by God's providence, though it feels like chance. Sometimes mercy arrives on a donkey, riding toward anger before anger arrives at the door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David speaks his grievance aloud: he has guarded Nabal's flocks faithfully, asked nothing, and been answered with scorn. 'He has returned me evil for good.' How many times have we felt this exact wound, and how hard it is to see past it to mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David makes a vow in anger—he will destroy Nabal's house entirely. His words are fierce and absolute. He has reached the place where a man decides to teach an unmistakable lesson. And then, without knowing it, he is about to be taught one himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abigail sees David and bows herself low to the ground. She has moved from taking care of provisions to taking care of a man's soul. She understands that David's real danger is not to Nabal—it is to himself, to his own future, to his own conscience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abigail places herself between David's anger and its target. 'On me be the blame,' she says. It is the language of substitution, of someone willing to bear the weight so that another may not have to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abigail speaks plainly about Nabal: his name means 'fool,' and folly is exactly what he is. But she does not ask David to kill a fool. She simply names the truth and moves the conversation away from what Nabal deserves, toward what David deserves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is Abigail's deepest wisdom: 'Yahweh has withheld you from blood guiltiness.' She sees what David cannot yet see in his anger—that he stands at a crossroads between justice and mercy, and that God's hand is still guiding him toward mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abigail offers her gift not as payment for safety, but as honor for the men who follow David. She frames it as respect for warriors, not as appeasement of anger. The angle of her mercy changes everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abigail speaks of God's promise: 'Yahweh will certainly make my lord a sure house.' She reminds David of who he really is—not a man bent on revenge, but a man whom God has chosen, who fights God's battles.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'The soul of my lord will be bound in the bundle of life with Yahweh your God.' Abigail uses the most intimate language of belonging to God. She promises David that his life is held secure in God's hand—not because of what he does, but because of who he is to God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abigail points to David's future: 'When Yahweh has appointed you prince over Israel.' She sees the calling God has placed on David's life—and reminds him that a man chosen to lead a nation cannot afford to be governed by anger toward a fool.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abigail asks David to remember his servant when he is king. She is not asking for reward, but for remembrance—for the chance to say one day that she stood in the gap when a good man nearly became a guilty one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's anger breaks like a wave against rock. He blesses God—not for victory, but for being sent someone wise enough to stop him. 'Blessed is Yahweh, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David praises Abigail's discretion—her ability to see clearly and act rightly. He acknowledges that she has kept him from blood guiltiness, from becoming the kind of man revenge makes of us. Her wisdom was his salvation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David speaks aloud what would have happened if Abigail had not come: destruction. But now he sees it as mercy that he did not do this thing. The price of his restraint is Abigail's courage, and God's hand holding him back from himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David accepts what Abigail has brought and sends her home in peace. He has heard her voice and granted her request—the greatest courtesy a man in power can show is to be changed by the wisdom of another.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nabal, drunk on wine and pride, celebrates his own feast while his wife saves his life. He does not know how close death came, how narrowly he escaped the consequences of his own folly. He lies in his ignorance, happy and doomed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the morning, when Abigail tells him, his heart 'dies within him.' He becomes 'as a stone.' He has learned at last the cost of his contempt. But the learning comes too late—it paralyzes him rather than changes him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten days later, Yahweh strikes Nabal, and he dies. God's judgment is silent, certain, and removed from human revenge. Nabal is not destroyed by David's sword, but by his own folly, and by God's hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David blesses God for pleading his cause. He recognizes that his reputation has been vindicated not by his own sword, but by God's justice. And now he turns his attention to Abigail—the woman who saved him from himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's servants come to Abigail with his proposal of marriage. What began as a moment of intervention becomes a union. Abigail moves from defending another's house to building her own with a man who respects her wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abigail's answer is humility itself: 'Your servant is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.' She recognizes that marriage to David is not about gaining status, but about serving a greater calling. She is ready.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abigail rises and rides on a donkey with her women, following David's messengers into her new life. The woman who rode down a mountain to stop a killing now rides toward a marriage. Both journeys come from the same courageous heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David also takes Ahinoam of Jezreel as a wife. David's life is becoming more complex, his household growing. Yet for all his multiplying loyalties, Abigail will remain a woman whose wisdom he treasures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul, meanwhile, has given David's wife Michal to another man. The political machinery grinds on, tearing apart what belonged together. Readers today hear an echo of how power tears at the bonds of love—and how God's mercy, like Abigail's, still interrupts the machinery.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
